title: Le Voyage au bout du corps — Marseille to Ivry
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: La blessure à la racine — Marseille & Smyrne

stops.name: Marseille — 4 rue du Jardin-des-Plantes
stops.campa: At eight in the morning Antoine Marie Joseph Artaud is born into the house on the rue du Jardin-des-Plantes, into Levantine blood: the father a ship-fitter of Marseille, the mother Euphrasie Nalpas, daughter of Smyrna. Two grandmothers, sisters born on the quays of the Aegean, stand at the root of the line like twin caryatids. The sea-trade city receives him; of nine children born to Euphrasie, only three will live. The one who lives this day is the one appointed to go to the end of the body.
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Marseille — the sickroom of the meningitis
stops.campa: In his fifth year the meningitis enters the child and nearly carries him off. The doctors give him up; the family keeps vigil; he returns from the border but not intact. The illness leaves its tithe: the stabbing pains of the head that will accompany him all his life, the tremors, the contracted nerves. This is the wound at the root — the first proof that his body has been claimed as a battlefield. Everything he later writes against the judgment of God begins in this bed in Marseille.
suggested_refs: Le Pèse-Nerfs — the testimony of the nerves
sources: Stephen Barber, Antonin Artaud: Blows and Bombs

stops.name: Smyrna — the grandmothers' city
stops.campa: The family crosses the sea to Smyrna, to the grandmother Mariette Nalpas, called Neneka, in the merchant city of the Levant. The child hears Greek and Turkish in the streets, the other tongue of his blood. Bathing off the coast he is taken by the water and nearly drowns; the sea gives him back a second time spared. Smyrna prints itself into him — the Orient at the root of the line — and Neneka will return at the end, at Ivry, as one of the daughters of the heart he summons around his bed.
suggested_refs: postcards of Smyrna before the fire of 1922
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Marseille — Collège du Sacré-Cœur
stops.campa: At the Jesuit collège of the Sacré-Cœur the boy founds a little review with his schoolfellows and signs his first poems Louis des Attides. The name is a mask and a prophecy: he will spend a life shedding names — Artaud, le Révélé, Nalpas, le Mômo — as a body sheds skins. He reads Baudelaire and Poe. The headaches keep their appointments. In the chapel the incense and the Latin enter him deeply enough that thirty years later, at Rodez, they will have to be torn out by force.

stops.name: Marseille — La Rougière, the first house of health
stops.campa: At eighteen the crisis comes. He destroys his manuscripts, gives away his books, falls into stammering and pain, and the family delivers him to the first maison de santé, La Rougière, outside Marseille. The sanatoria adolescence begins: five years passed from house to house while other boys pass through the trenches. The institutions take his youth the way the asylums will later take his middle age; he is already learning the geography of confinement that is the dark half of this journey.
suggested_refs: records of the maisons de santé, 1915-1920
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Digne — the two months of the soldier
stops.campa: Conscripted, he is posted to the infantry at Digne in the mountains of Provence. The army holds him nine months and then opens its hand: discharged — for sleepwalking, the tradition says, though the true cause is the whole condition of him. The war that devours his generation refuses him; he is reserved for another front. He walks out of the barracks already a veteran of an invisible campaign whose communiqués will be the letters, the manifestos, the screams recorded thirty years later.

stops.name: Le Chanet, Neuchâtel — the pact of laudanum
stops.campa: In the Swiss sanatorium of Le Chanet, above Neuchâtel, Dr Dardel treats the young man's head-pains with laudanum. The tincture of opium enters the economy of his body and never leaves it: the pact is signed here, in clean mountain air, on medical paper. Opium will be his crutch, his tax, his one mercy through asylums and detoxifications, until at the very end the doctors of Ivry, having found the cancer, return it to him without limit. Dardel also counsels Paris and the theatre. Both prescriptions take.
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Villejuif — the house of Dr Toulouse
stops.campa: Artaud comes up to Paris and is entrusted to Dr Édouard Toulouse, alienist of Villejuif, who studies superior men as others study minerals. Toulouse recognizes at once what has arrived in his ward: not a patient but a case of genius, and he sets him to editing his review Demain. Paris in 1920 is a city rebuilding its nerves; Artaud, twenty-three, enters it through the door of an asylum — the same door, at Ivry, through which he will leave the world twenty-eight years later.
suggested_refs: the review Demain, edited by Artaud

stops.name: Théâtre de l'Œuvre — first stage
stops.campa: Lugné-Poe, the old master of symbolism who once launched Ubu Roi upon the world, gives Artaud his first role at the Théâtre de l'Œuvre. It is a bit part; it is also an ordination. The theatre that scandalized the fathers receives the son who will out-scandalize them all. From this small stage the line runs straight through Jarry — whose name Artaud will raise on his own theatre six years hence — to the Theatre of Cruelty. He steps into the light and the light takes his measure.
suggested_refs: programmes of the Théâtre de l'Œuvre, 1921

stops.name: Théâtre de l'Atelier, place Dullin — the actor who plays with his organs
stops.campa: He joins Charles Dullin's Atelier on the hill of Montmartre, school of improvisation, mask and Oriental gesture. Cast as the emperor Charlemagne he approaches the throne on all fours, a beast of majesty; reproached, he rises with disdain: ah, if you want verisimilitude. Dullin says of him that he acts with his organs — the phrase is exact, a diagnosis and a manifesto. Here too he meets Génica Athanasiou, the Romanian actress, the one long love of his body. Every doctrine of the Theatre of Cruelty is already present in this apprentice.
suggested_refs: photographs of Artaud in Atelier productions, 1922

stops.name: 3 rue de Grenelle — the letters to Jacques Rivière
stops.campa: He sends poems to the Nouvelle Revue Française and Rivière, the editor, refuses them — then asks to meet the man. From the refusal grows the correspondence that founds the canon: Artaud describes, with clinical exactitude, the erosion of his own thought, the mind that abandons him at every degree, and offers the description itself as the work. Rivière, shaken, publishes the letters in place of the poems. Literature has been shown its own outside. The dossier of the case of Antonin Artaud is opened here and never closed.
stops.quote: Je souffre d'une effroyable maladie de l'esprit. Ma pensée m'abandonne à tous les degrés.
stops.quote_source: Correspondance avec Jacques Rivière, lettre du 5 juin 1923

stops.name: 15 rue de Grenelle — the Bureau of Surrealist Researches
stops.campa: Breton hands Artaud the direction of the Bureau de recherches surréalistes, the storefront office where dreams are taken down like depositions. Artaud turns it into a chancellery of war: he drafts the Address to the Pope, the Address to the Dalai Lama, the Letter to the Rectors of the European Universities — communiqués of the spirit to the seated powers of the earth. The third number of La Révolution surréaliste, made under his hand, is the most incendiary thing the movement ever prints. For one season the Surrealist revolution speaks with his voice.

stops.name: Paris — L'Ombilic des Limbes
stops.campa: The NRF publishes L'Ombilic des Limbes, and with Le Pèse-Nerfs the same year, the book of his body enters the world: not poems but nerve-scales, weighings of anguish, a literature that declares itself the residue of a man and not his ornament. He states the law of the whole canon — where others offer works, he shows his mind. The books are thin as knives. Readers who open them are not reading; they are being operated upon. The theatre he has not yet named is already written here.
stops.quote: Là où d'autres proposent des œuvres, je ne prétends pas autre chose que de montrer mon esprit.
suggested_refs: first editions of L'Ombilic des Limbes and Le Pèse-Nerfs

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt — Marat in Gance's Napoléon
stops.campa: In Abel Gance's colossal Napoléon Artaud is Marat, the friend of the people, burning in his bath. He does not play the revolutionary; he is possessed by him, the eyes enormous, the face a blade. Gance's cameras, unchained from their tripods, swing like censers around him. Of all the faces in that imperial liturgy his is the one that looks back out of the revolution itself. The cinema years begin: the screen takes his face the way the asylums will later take his body, and keeps it.
suggested_refs: Abel Gance, Napoléon (1927) — Artaud as Marat

stops.name: Café Le Prophète — the expulsion
stops.campa: The Surrealists convene their tribunal in a café and expel Antonin Artaud. The charge: he pursues the revolution of the spirit alone, refuses the party, insists on theatre — he is, in the exact sense, too absolute even for them. Breton pronounces; the pamphlet Au grand jour will nail the sentence up in print. Artaud answers with À la grande nuit ou le bluff surréaliste: it is they who have abandoned the absolute. The movement that mapped the interior casts out the only member who lived there. He walks on alone, excommunicated, intact.
suggested_refs: À la grande nuit ou le bluff surréaliste (1927)

segments.name: Le théâtre et son double — cinéma, Jarry, Cruauté

stops.name: Opéra de Paris — the triple screen
stops.campa: Napoléon premieres at the Opéra on three screens wide as the horizon, before the President of the Republic. Marat's assassinated face, Artaud's face, is projected at the scale of a cathedral wall upon the assembled dignity of France. He sits in the house watching himself die in his bath, larger than the state. It is the highest official altitude his image will ever reach — twenty-one years before another organ of that same state, the radio, bans his voice on the eve of broadcast.
suggested_refs: the polyvision triptych of Napoléon at the Opéra, 7 April 1927

stops.name: Théâtre de Grenelle — first night of the Théâtre Alfred Jarry
stops.campa: With Roger Vitrac and Robert Aron he raises the standard of the Théâtre Alfred Jarry, named for the father of Ubu, and gives its first performance: his own Ventre brûlé ou la mère folle among the offerings. No subsidy, no house of its own, four programmes in three years, every one a skirmish — the Surrealists come to heckle their excommunicate, and the police attend. It is theatre as raid, rehearsal for the doctrine: the stage exists to endanger, once, unrepeatably, everyone in the room.
suggested_refs: Théâtre Alfred Jarry manifestos and programmes, 1926-1930

stops.name: Studios de Billancourt — the monk Massieu, facing Rouen
stops.campa: On Dreyer's plaster Rouen, Artaud is the young monk Massieu in La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc, the one merciful face of that film, bending toward Falconetti's Joan through the whole geometry of her judges. Dreyer shoots the faces naked, without makeup, in the order of the trial itself; Falconetti burns and Artaud pities. This stop faces two ways: toward her journey and toward Joan's own trial at Rouen in 1431 — the saint condemned by the tribunals of God, whom Artaud serves here in effigy before enduring her process in his own flesh at Dublin, at Rodez.
suggested_refs: Carl Th. Dreyer, La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928) — Massieu beside Falconetti
the trial of Joan of Arc, Rouen, 1431

stops.name: Théâtre de l'Avenue — the scandal of the Dream Play
stops.campa: The Théâtre Alfred Jarry mounts Strindberg's Dream Play, paid for by Swedish patrons. The Surrealists descend upon the house to break the evening; Artaud, to outflank them, denounces his own patrons from the stage. Police cordon the second performance and Breton is barred at the door. The production dies of its wounds; the friendship of the movement is ash. Artaud has demonstrated the theorem he will spend a life proving: a true performance is indistinguishable from a riot, and the author is the first casualty.
suggested_refs: Le Songe, Théâtre Alfred Jarry, June 1928 — police reports and press

stops.name: NRF, rue de Grenelle — the First Manifesto of the Theatre of Cruelty
stops.campa: The Nouvelle Revue Française prints Le Théâtre de la Cruauté, first manifesto. Artaud has seen the Balinese dancers at the Colonial Exposition and recognized theatre in its sacred state: a language of space, of cries, of hieroglyphs made with the body. He decrees the end of the tyranny of the text and the return of the plague, of danger, of metaphysics that enters through the skin. The essays gather toward Le Théâtre et son double, the book that will re-arm the stages of the earth for a century.
stops.quote: Sans un élément de cruauté à la base de tout spectacle, le théâtre n'est pas possible.
suggested_refs: the Balinese theatre at the Exposition coloniale, 1931

stops.name: Sorbonne, amphithéâtre — Le Théâtre et la Peste
stops.campa: Invited to lecture on the theatre and the plague, Artaud abandons his pages and becomes the thing itself. Before the learned of the Sorbonne he enacts the plague entering a body — his own — the face contorting, the throat strangling, the death performed to its end on the platform. The hall empties in laughter and fright; Anaïs Nin remains and writes down what she has seen. He wipes his face and goes out into the wet street with her, having delivered the only lecture of its kind ever given: the argument as agony.
stops.quote: I want to give them the experience itself, the plague itself, so they will be terrified and awaken.
stops.quote_source: Anaïs Nin, Diary, April 1933 (recording Artaud's words)
suggested_refs: Anaïs Nin's diary account of 6 April 1933

stops.name: Folies-Wagram — Les Cenci
stops.campa: The Theatre of Cruelty gives its single full-scale battle: Les Cenci, after Shelley and Stendhal — incest, parricide, the wheel. Artaud directs and plays the monstrous father; Balthus builds the ruins; Iya Abdy shines; recorded bells and storms assault the house from all sides, the first spatialized sound in the French theatre. Seventeen performances, and the money fails. The defeat is total and it is a liberation: the stage of Paris has refused him, so he will seek the theatre at its source, among peoples who never separated it from rite. Mexico is already forming.

segments.name: La montagne des signes — Mexique & Ciguri

stops.name: Antwerp — embarkation on the Albertville
stops.campa: In the North Sea winter Artaud boards the Albertville at Antwerp, bound for the Americas with a mission from the ministry and almost no money. He goes, he says, to seek in Mexico the last living root of a culture that still holds magic to be exact science — to flee a Europe whose civilization has separated itself from the body. The manifestos are behind him; the mountain is ahead. He is thirty-nine. The gangway at Antwerp is the true frontier of this journey: after it, the signs begin.
sources: Letras Libres, Antonin Artaud en México

stops.name: Havana — the sorcerer's little sword
stops.campa: The ship pauses five days at Havana. There, at a santería gathering, a Black sorcerer places in Artaud's hands a small sword of Toledo steel with a hooked hilt of three fish-forms. It is the first of the two talismans — the sword and, a year later, the cane of Saint Patrick — the two magical objects to which he will identify his being and his destiny. He carries it into the sierra and to the priests of the sun, and will name it in the letter that announces the revelation of the sign.
suggested_refs: the Toledo sword of Havana — the first talisman

stops.name: Veracruz — landing in Mexico
stops.campa: On 7 February Artaud steps ashore at Veracruz, port of the conquest, and takes the road of Cortés inland — but he comes to reverse the conquest, to ask the Indian earth for what Europe burned. Mexico in 1936 is a republic of muralists and revolutionaries who preach the machine and the proletariat; Artaud arrives preaching the opposite: that the revolution must be a revolution of the body, and that the old solar culture buried under the republic is the only physician for the sickness of the world.
sources: Letras Libres, Antonin Artaud en México

stops.name: Mexico City — the lectures at San Ildefonso
stops.campa: In the old college of San Ildefonso, under the murals of Orozco, Artaud lectures: Surrealism and Revolution, Man against Destiny, The Theatre and the Gods. He tells the youth of Mexico that Europe is a corpse that exports its death, and that Mexico's task is not to imitate Marx but to disinter its own sun. He writes for El Nacional through the months that follow, poor, seeking peyote and the sierra. The capital listens politely to the prophet; the mountain, which does not read newspapers, is preparing to receive him properly.
sources: Letras Libres, Antonin Artaud en México

stops.name: Chihuahua — the rail-head of the sierra
stops.campa: At the end of August, with a government grant of last resort, Artaud takes the train north to Chihuahua, gateway of the Sierra Tarahumara. Here he performs the act that measures the whole pilgrimage: he undergoes his final detoxification and gives up the last of the heroin, on a mountain path, days from any relief — for the peyote must find the body unoccupied. Sick, shaking, held on his horse, he turns toward the high country of the Rarámuri. Twelve days of ascent stand between him and the land of signs.
suggested_refs: D'un voyage au pays des Tarahumaras
sources: Otro Ángulo, Artaud en la Sierra Tarahumara

stops.name: The ascent — la Montagne des signes
stops.campa: Climbing into the sierra Artaud sees that the mountain itself is written. Rocks carved into heads that answer one another, drowned men half-eaten by stone, a naked man leaning from a window of rock — the same forms repeating at intervals too exact for chance. The land of the Tarahumara is full of signs, and he reads them as the gods' signatures set out along the road of the rite. The journey has passed out of geography: from this ridge onward every stone is a sentence and the traveler is being read in return.
stops.quote: Le pays des Tarahumaras est plein de signes, de formes, d'effigies naturelles qui ne semblent point nés du hasard.
stops.quote_source: La Montagne des signes, in Les Tarahumaras

stops.name: Norogachic — among the Rarámuri
stops.campa: At Norogachic, high in the sierra, Artaud lodges among the Rarámuri, the running people, and petitions the priests of the sun for the rite. They make him wait — weeks of maize, cold and refusal, for the peyote is not given to the curious. He watches the Tutuguri, the rite of the sun's rising, the sacrificed bulls and the crosses that are not Christian crosses but older instruments of orientation. The Indians study this gaunt European who has thrown away his drugs to be worthy; the mountain deliberates his case.
suggested_refs: Tutuguri, le rite du soleil noir
sources: Otro Ángulo, Artaud en la Sierra Tarahumara

stops.name: The rite of Ciguri — the dance of the peyote
stops.campa: The priests consent. Through a night and a day the sorcerers grate the peyote root over the fire, the rasping-sticks speak, the dancers stamp the crossed earth of the ceremonial ground, and Artaud, kneeling where the mirror flashes and the staffs are planted, receives Ciguri. The initiation is taken whole: he sees the organs of his body sorted and judged, the false Artaud burned away, the self led back to the source it had lost. Twelve days of rite, the fulfilment of the voyage and the standard against which all his later crucifixions are measured.
stops.quote: Le Peyotl ramène le moi à ses sources vraies.
stops.quote_source: Le Rite du Peyotl chez les Tarahumaras
suggested_refs: Le Rite du Peyotl chez les Tarahumaras

stops.name: Saint-Nazaire — return on the Mexique
stops.campa: He boards the Mexique at Veracruz on the last day of October and lands at Saint-Nazaire on 12 November, carrying the sierra inside him and the little sword in his baggage. Europe receives back a man who has been reassembled by other hands than hers. He returns to Paris, to poverty, to a last attempt at ordinary happiness — the engagement to Cécile Schramme of Brussels. But a man who has taken Ciguri does not resume; the signs he learned to read in the mountain now begin arriving in France, addressed to him.
sources: Letras Libres, Antonin Artaud en México

segments.name: La canne de saint Patrick — Bruxelles & l'Irlande

stops.name: Paris — the cane given by René Thomas
stops.campa: The young Breton friend René Thomas places in Artaud's hands a knotted cane of dark wood. Artaud knows it at once and entirely: this is the staff of Saint Patrick, the Bachall Ísu, staff of Jesus himself, thirteen knots for thirteen ages — the second talisman, twin to the Havana sword. He writes to Cécile Schramme of the revelation of the sign: the sword and the cane are now the two magical objects that complete him. He walks Paris striking the pavement with it. The prophecies begin; they will not stop again.
suggested_refs: the cane of Saint Patrick — the lost second talisman
sources: Come Here To Me, Artaud and the staff of Saint Patrick

stops.name: Brussels, Maison d'Art — the broken engagement
stops.campa: Invited by his fiancée's family to lecture at the Maison d'Art, Artaud mounts the platform before the Brussels bourgeoisie and detonates. The accounts diverge — the decomposition of Paris, his Mexico, obscenities hurled like anathemas; what is certain is the scandal. The tramway director's daughter cannot marry this. Within days the engagement with Cécile Schramme is broken, the last door into ordinary life closed by his own voice. He returns to Paris with the cane and the sword, unencumbered now, as a projectile is unencumbered.
suggested_refs: accounts of the Maison d'Art lecture, May 1937
sources: Cairn, Avatars du nom propre chez Artaud

stops.name: Paris — Les Nouvelles Révélations de l'Être
stops.campa: Denoël publishes a slim prophetic tract signed not Artaud but LE RÉVÉLÉ. Cast by the tarot and the numbers, it announces the destruction of the present world by fire and water, the coming of the Tortured One who will reveal all things. The author has erased his name because the name was a garment and the garment has burned. Paris shrugs at one more pamphlet. But the tract is a sailing-schedule: the Revealed One has computed where the staff must be returned, and the island of Saint Patrick is waiting.

stops.name: Cobh — landfall in Ireland
stops.campa: On 14 August Artaud lands at Cobh, the deep-water port of Cork, carrying the staff of Saint Patrick home to Ireland. He has almost no English, no Irish, and a letter asking the Irish state to receive the relic and the man. The mission is exact in his mind: to return the Bachall Ísu to its island before the world's judgment, of which he is the herald. Ireland, Catholic and new-sovereign, does not yet know that its saint's staff has entered the country in the fist of a French prophet.
suggested_refs: Artaud 1937 Apocalypse — the letters from Ireland

stops.name: Galway — toward the islands
stops.campa: From Cork he comes to Galway, the grey stone city facing the Atlantic, and takes lodging while the money thins. Across the bay lie the Aran Islands, the bare limestone rafts where the old tongue and the old faith are still whole — the westernmost stones of Europe, and therefore, by the geometry of his prophecy, the proper anteroom of the world's end. He buys passage on the island boat. Behind him the letters begin to fly to Paris, each one heavier with doom than the last.

stops.name: Kilronan, Inishmore — among the fishermen
stops.campa: On Inishmore, largest of the Arans, Artaud lodges at Kilronan among fishermen who speak Irish and take him for a strange, courteous, penniless pilgrim. By day he strides the island with the staff; by night he writes the letters of doom to Paris — to Breton, to Paulhan: the world will be destroyed by fire, the Antichrist reigns, he himself is the instrument of the reckoning; he signs with new names and encloses spells. The islanders feed him on credit. The Atlantic repeats its one grey prophecy against the pier.

stops.name: Eoghanacht & Dún Aonghasa — the western rampart
stops.campa: He walks west to the hamlet of Eoghanacht and stands at Dún Aonghasa, the prehistoric fort whose half-ring of walls breaks off at a sheer cliff over the open Atlantic. It is the last architecture of Europe, a theatre whose fourth wall is the end of the world — the exact stage his doctrine always demanded. The staff of the saint touches the stones of the pagans. Here the itinerary of the journey reaches its westernmost point; every step after this cliff is a step toward the asylums.

stops.name: Dublin — destitute
stops.campa: The credit of the islands exhausted, Artaud crosses to Dublin with nothing. He sleeps where the destitute sleep, seeks out priests and ministries to deliver the staff into the hands of the Irish church, and is turned from door to door — a gaunt foreigner with burning eyes, no money and a stick he calls the staff of Christ. Somewhere in these days the cane leaves his hands and passes out of history; no man has seen it since. The prophet is now unarmed in a city preparing to expel him.
suggested_refs: the lost Bachall Ísu — last seen Dublin, September 1937
sources: Come Here To Me, Artaud and the staff of Saint Patrick

stops.name: Milltown Park — the arrest at the Jesuit house
stops.campa: Seeking refuge, Artaud comes to Milltown Park, the Jesuit house in the south of the city, and will not be turned away; the fathers call the Garda. He is taken in the grounds, held at Donnybrook station, then lodged six days in Mountjoy Prison as a destitute and undesirable alien. In the prison of the Irish republic the man who carried their saint's staff back to them sits in a cell — the first cell of the eleven years of cells. The state signs the deportation order without ever learning what it is deporting.
sources: Come Here To Me, Artaud and the staff of Saint Patrick

stops.name: Cobh — deported aboard the Washington
stops.campa: On 29 September the SS Washington steams out of Cobh with Artaud aboard, expelled from the island he came to save. At sea, when crewmen enter his cabin bearing tools, he reads assassination in their hands and defends himself; he is overpowered, bound and put in the straitjacket. He will say ever after that he was attacked and that the jacket was the beginning of the great bewitchment. The ship carries him toward Le Havre as cargo. The journey of the staff ends as a Passion begins: bound, silenced, delivered to the authorities.

stops.name: Le Havre — the first station
stops.campa: Landed at Le Havre in the straitjacket, Artaud is committed to the general hospital and held in a barred cell. No one tells his family for weeks; he simply vanishes from the world between one tide and the next. In the cell he is assailed by visions: friends murdered outside his window, Génica and Anne Manson calling to him through the walls. The nine years of the asylum stations begin here, at the water's edge — France receives back her poet and books him in as an unknown madman off an American ship.

stops.name: Quatre-Mares, Sotteville-lès-Rouen — the second station
stops.campa: He is transferred to the asylum of Quatre-Mares at Sotteville-lès-Rouen, into the men's ward, matricule among matricules. Here his mother finds him at last after months of searching — he does not know her, or will not; the bewitchment has eaten the names. The letters from Quatre-Mares mask his identity under borrowed names and cry out with an extraordinary energy against the machinery that holds him. Across the river lies Rouen, where Joan was burned; the monk Massieu of the film is now himself in the hands of the judges.

stops.name: Sainte-Anne, Paris — Lacan pronounces
stops.campa: Moved to Sainte-Anne in Paris, Artaud is held in the secure ward while, that same February, Gallimard at last publishes Le Théâtre et son double — the book appears while its author is behind asylum walls, and he does not learn of it. The young Dr Jacques Lacan examines him and pronounces the case: fixed — obsessed, finished, he will live to eighty and never write another line. The oracle of the new science is exact in everything except the truth: the patient has before him the most volcanic decade of writing in the French language.
suggested_refs: Le Théâtre et son double, first edition (février 1938)
Roger Blin's account of Lacan's verdict

stops.name: Ville-Évrard — the hunger years, signed Antonin Nalpas
stops.campa: On 27 February 1939 he enters Ville-Évrard, east of Paris, for four years. The war comes and the asylums of occupied France starve; around him the mad die of hunger by the thousand, the great silent massacre of the institutions. He signs his letters Antonin Nalpas, his mother's blood-name — Artaud, he explains, is dead, and the dead man's name must not be used. From the ward he mails the sorts, spell-drawings burned and pierced, to protect the few he loves and to strike his enemies. Génica visits and finds a skeleton that prophesies.

stops.name: Chezal-Benoît — the ruse of the transfer
stops.campa: Robert Desnos, who cannot bear what Ville-Évrard is doing to him, arranges the rescue: a transfer south toward the free zone, to the asylum of his friend Ferdière at Rodez. On 22 January 1943 Artaud is moved to Chezal-Benoît in the Cher, the way-station where the paperwork crosses the demarcation line. He weighs little more than a child. Desnos himself will die in the camps two years later; his last great act of friendship is this file of forms that carries a starving poet out of the death-zone of the northern asylums.
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Rodez — arrival at the asylum of Dr Ferdière
stops.campa: On 11 February 1943 Artaud enters the asylum of Rodez in the Aveyron, and Dr Gaston Ferdière — psychiatrist, poet, friend of the Surrealists — receives him at his own table. There is food here, and books, and a doctor who knows his work. Artaud arrives in the grip of the great possession, blessing and exorcising, genuflecting in the corridors; he is for a season fervently Christian, singing litanies against his demons. Ferdière undertakes to give him back to literature — and reaches, among his instruments, for the new machine.
suggested_refs: Ferdière's memoirs of Artaud at Rodez

stops.name: Rodez — the electroshocks: fifty-one comas
stops.campa: On 20 June 1943 the first series begins. Strapped to the table, Artaud is put through the electroshock: series upon series across eighteen months, fifty-one comas by his own unwavering count — the crucifixions of the machine. One session breaks a vertebra. He describes dying under the current and wandering ninety minutes outside his body while the attendants prepared the mortuary basket. And out of the broken ground the work erupts: the notebooks begin, the drawings begin, the glossolalia pours forth — invented tongues that he declares true speech, older than French, the language of the body before the theft.
stops.quote: Or je suis mort à Rodez, sous l'électrochoc.
suggested_refs: letters to Dr Ferdière and Dr Latrémolière
sources: Cairn, L'introduction de l'électrochoc dans les hôpitaux psychiatriques français

stops.name: Rodez — the apostasy and the tongues
stops.campa: In the spring of 1945 the Christian period ends in violent apostasy: Artaud renounces his baptism, spits out the God he had sung litanies to, and declares the sacraments the oldest of the bewitchments. Christ, communion, the Virgin — machinery of the theft of the body. The Cahiers fill at the rate of possession, hundreds of pages a month; the great pencil portraits and the totemic drawings come; the glossolalia hardens into a liturgy of his own. To Henri Parisot he writes the Letters from Rodez, the doctrine of the man remade: poetry is not written, it is lived.
stops.quote: Si je suis poète ou acteur, ce n'est pas pour écrire ou déclamer des poésies, mais pour les vivre.
stops.quote_source: Lettres de Rodez, à Henri Parisot (1945)

stops.name: Ivry-sur-Seine — the clinic of Dr Delmas
stops.campa: Freed from Rodez on 25 May 1946, Artaud reaches Paris the next day and enters the maison de santé of Dr Achille Delmas at Ivry-sur-Seine — a resident now, not a prisoner; the gate is open and the key is his. Delmas indulges him in everything, the laudanum included. In the overgrown garden Artaud finds a derelict hunting pavilion, older than the clinic, and chooses it over the comfortable rooms: a cold outbuilding with no lock on the door. There he installs the block of wood he hammers while he writes, and begins the last two years.
sources: Van Gogh le suicidé de la société (Wikipédia notice)

stops.name: Théâtre Sarah-Bernhardt — the homage
stops.campa: On 7 June the theatre of Sarah Bernhardt fills for the Homage to Antonin Artaud: Breton speaks his reconciliation, Gide has come, Jouvet, Barrault, Blin and the actors give his texts to the dark house — by his own wish Artaud is not in the hall. The theatre weeps for the man the age had buried alive. Twenty years of quarrels dissolve in a single evening of restitution; the excommunicate of 1926 is received back as a father of the tribe. The proceeds are laid at his feet like arms at a survivor's.
suggested_refs: Breton's Hommage à Antonin Artaud (7 juin 1946)

stops.name: Galerie Pierre — the auction of the manuscripts
stops.campa: At Pierre Loeb's gallery on the rue des Beaux-Arts the friends hold the sale: Picasso, Braque, Giacometti, Dubuffet and the others have given paintings and sculptures, the writers have given manuscripts, and the auction of 13 June turns the homage into bread and opium money. The tract announcing it reads like a bulletin of state — the nation of painters and poets taxing itself for its prophet. With the proceeds a fund is built to keep him; France, which locked him up by prefectural order, now ransoms him by subscription.
suggested_refs: Hommage à Antonin Artaud — tract and sale catalogue, June 1946
sources: INHA, Hommage à Antonin Artaud, vente du 13 juin 1946

stops.name: Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier — Artaud le Mômo before the world
stops.campa: The posters read: Histoire vécue d'Artaud-Mômo — Tête-à-tête par Antonin Artaud. On 13 January the Vieux-Colombier is crammed — Gide, Camus, Breton, Paulhan, the whole intelligence of Paris — to see the returned one. For three hours he reads, screams, loses his pages, seizes his face, and finally the poems scatter from his hands and he stops, mid-performance, stripped before them: the collapse itself becomes the performance, the exact theatre of cruelty enacted in his person. Gide embraces him on the stage. Afterward he swears it: he will never read in public again.
suggested_refs: accounts of the Vieux-Colombier séance (Gide, in Combat)
sources: Déméter, La conférence d'Artaud au Vieux-Colombier
INA, La conférence d'Artaud au Vieux-Colombier

stops.name: Musée de l'Orangerie — before the Van Goghs
stops.campa: At the Orangerie the Van Gogh exhibition is hung, and Artaud walks through it — one suicided of society before the canvases of another. He has just read a psychiatrist's article calling Van Gogh a degenerate; standing in the wheat and the crows he recognizes the whole crime: the painter was not mad, he was lucid past bearing, and society strangled him through its doctors. In days of fury at Ivry he dictates and hammers out the answer, the essay that will be crowned within the year. The alienated one writes the trial of the alienists.
stops.quote: Personne n'a jamais écrit ou peint, sculpté, modelé, construit, inventé, que pour sortir en fait de l'enfer.
stops.quote_source: Van Gogh le suicidé de la société
sources: Van Gogh le suicidé de la société (K éditeur, 1947)

stops.name: Galerie Pierre — Portraits et dessins par Antonin Artaud
stops.campa: In July the Galerie Pierre shows what the asylums could not prevent: the portraits. Faces of his friends drawn as if trepanned — pierced, seamed, nailed with graphite, the features rebuilt after the judgment of God has been subtracted from them. For the catalogue he writes that the human face is an empty force, a field of death, which the painter's work must resurrect by giving it back its own features. The drawings of a certified madman hang in the capital of painting, and painting is instructed by them.
stops.quote: Le visage humain est en effet une force vide, un champ de mort.
stops.quote_source: Le Visage humain (texte pour l'exposition, juillet 1947)
suggested_refs: the 1946-48 portraits (Paule Thévenin, Jacques Prevel, Colette Thomas)

stops.name: Studios de la Radiodiffusion, rue François-Ier — recording the judgment
stops.campa: Between 22 and 29 November, in the studios of the French Radio, Artaud records Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu with Maria Casarès, Roger Blin and Paule Thévenin. Between the texts he screams; he beats drums and xylophone; the glossolalia goes onto the state's own magnetic tape. America stockpiling sperm for its wars, the god found on the autopsy table, the body to be remade without organs — the whole doctrine, scored for voice and percussion. It is his final work and he knows it: the theatre of cruelty achieved at last, by radio, addressed to everyone at once.
stops.quote: Car liez-moi si vous le voulez, mais il n'y a rien de plus inutile qu'un organe.
stops.quote_source: Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu
suggested_refs: the INA recording of Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu
INA, Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu, version finale

stops.name: Radiodiffusion française — the ban
stops.campa: The broadcast is set for the second of February. On the first, Wladimir Porché, director-general of the French Radio, forbids it — the night before transmission: the last censorship. A jury of writers and artists is convened days later in the studio, hears the work entire, and votes for its broadcast; the director holds the ban regardless. Artaud writes his letters of protest and then, with terrible calm, concludes that where the judgment of God reigns his voice cannot pass. The tape is locked in the state's vault, where it waits, like a relic, a quarter of a century.
suggested_refs: Artaud's letters to Wladimir Porché and René Guignard, February 1948
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, Pour en finir avec le jugement de dieu

stops.name: Ivry — the crowning and the sentence
stops.campa: In the same days two verdicts arrive at the pavilion. The Prix Sainte-Beuve is given to Van Gogh le suicidé de la société — the madman crowned by the critics for the book that indicts the doctors. And the doctors themselves, called for his pains, find the cancer, inoperable, deep in the body that has carried him to the end of itself. They do not tell him the name of it; they tell him he may have laudanum now without limit, and he understands the sentence inside the mercy. He keeps writing. The notebooks do not slow.
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, Van Gogh le suicidé de la société

stops.name: The pavilion at Ivry — dawn of 4 March 1948
stops.campa: At dawn on the fourth of March the gardener of the clinic brings breakfast to the pavilion and finds him at the foot of the bed, seated upright on the floor, one shoe in his hand — as if arrested midway between lying down and setting out, shod for one foot of the road. He is fifty-one. Alone, unwitnessed, without sacrament or doctor, the man who went to the end of the body has gone the one step past it. On the table the notebooks lie open; the last pages speak of the men who steal the bodies of the living.
stops.quote: Moi, Antonin Artaud, je suis mon fils, mon père, ma mère, et moi.
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud

stops.name: Cimetière d'Ivry — the grave
stops.campa: On 8 March they bury him in the cemetery of Ivry, and by his known will there is no priest at the grave: the apostate of Rodez is not handed back to the sacraments he tore out of himself. The friends stand in the March cold — the actors, the painters, the young poets who carried his notebooks. Later the body is translated south to Marseille, to the cimetière Saint-Pierre, into the earth of the Levantine blood where the journey opened. The circle closes: Marseille to Ivry, and Marseille again; the canon — the Œuvres complètes, the Tarahumara texts, the Rodez letters, the banned tape — remains above ground, unkillable.
suggested_refs: the grave at cimetière Saint-Pierre, Marseille
sources: Florence de Mèredieu, C'était Antonin Artaud
